**Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on Surah 112, verses 1–4 (part 1 of 2)**

It is Meccan according to Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, Ata', Ikrimah and Jabir, and Medinan according to one of the two opinions attributed to Ibn Abbas, and to Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Khuzaymah, Ibn Abi Asim in *al-Sunnah*, al-Baghawi in his *Mu'jam*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-Azamah*, and al-Hakim (who declared it sahih) narrated, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* reported, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that: "The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'O Muhammad, trace for us the lineage of your Lord.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born﴾, to the end. 'Nothing that is born does not die, and nothing that dies does not leave an inheritor. Allah neither dies nor is inherited.' ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾. He said: 'There was no one similar to Him or equal to Him, and there is nothing like unto Him.'" Al-Tirmidhi narrated it through another route from Abu al-Aliyah as a *mursal* report (one whose chain omits a companion), without mentioning Ubayy, and then said: "And this is more sound (asahh)."

Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Jabir, who said: "A Bedouin came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Trace for us the lineage of your Lord.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ to the end of the surah." Al-Suyuti judged its chain to be good (hasan).

Al-Tabarani and Abu al-Shaykh in *al-Azamah* narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The Quraysh said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Trace for us the lineage of your Lord,' so this surah was revealed: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Adi, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa al-Sifat* narrated from Ibn Abbas that "the Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ), among them Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and said: 'O Muhammad, describe for us your Lord who sent you.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge.﴾ ﴿He neither begets, so that a child should come forth from Him, nor is He born, so that anything should come forth from Him.﴾"

Abu Ubayd in *Fada'il al-Qur'an*, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i in *'Amal al-Yawm wa al-Laylah*, Ibn Mani', Muhammad ibn Nasr, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Diya in *al-Mukhtarah* narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ has recited a third of the Qur'an."

Ibn al-Durays, al-Bazzar, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ two hundred times, Allah will forgive him the sins of two hundred years."

Al-Bazzar said: "We do not know of anyone who narrated it from Anas except al-Hasan ibn Abi Ja'far and al-Aghlab ibn Tamim, and both are close in their poor memory."

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Durays, and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* narrated from Anas: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'I love this surah, ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Your love for it has admitted you to Paradise.'"

Ibn al-Durays, Abu Ya'la, and Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif* narrated from Anas, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Can none of you manage to recite ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ three times in a night? It is equal to a third of the Qur'an.'" Its chain is weak (da'if).

Muhammad ibn Nasr and Abu Ya'la narrated from Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ fifty times, the sins of fifty years will be forgiven him." Its chain is weak.

Al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Adi, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ two hundred times, Allah will record for him one thousand five hundred good deeds and erase from him the sins of fifty years, unless he has a debt." Its chain includes Hatim ibn Maymun, whom al-Bukhari and others declared weak. The wording of al-Tirmidhi is: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ two hundred times in a day, the sins of fifty years will be erased from him, unless he has a debt." Its chain also includes the same Hatim ibn Maymun.

Al-Tirmidhi, Muhammad ibn Nasr, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Adi, and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever wishes to sleep on his bed at night, and sleeps on his right side, then recites ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ one hundred times, then on the Day of Resurrection the Lord will say to him: 'O My servant, enter Paradise by your right side.'" Its chain also includes the same Hatim ibn Maymun.

After narrating it, al-Tirmidhi said: "It is gharib (unusual) from the hadith of Thabit," and "it has been narrated through a route other than this one from him."

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn al-Durays, Abu Ya'la, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* narrated from Anas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was in Syria, and in another wording, in Tabuk, when Jibril descended and said: 'O Muhammad, Mu'awiyah ibn Mu'awiyah al-Muzani has died. Would you like to pray over him?' He said: 'Yes.' So Jibril struck the earth with his wing, and everything humbled itself before him and clung to the earth, and his bier was raised for him, and he prayed over him. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'By what was Mu'awiyah given this virtue, that two rows of angels, each row of six thousand angels, prayed over him?' He said: 'By his recitation of ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, which he used to recite standing, sitting, coming, going, and sleeping.'" Its chain includes al-'Ala' ibn Muhammad al-Thaqafi, who is accused of fabricating hadith (matruk/muttaham bi al-wad').

It is also narrated through another route, longer than this, and its chain includes this same accused narrator.

There are other hadiths on this theme and on other matters in this chapter. It has been narrated through other routes that it is equal to a third of the Qur'an, and among these narrations some are sahih and some are hasan. Among them is what Muslim, al-Tirmidhi (who declared it sahih), and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Gather together, for I will recite to you a third of the Qur'an." So whoever gathered, gathered. Then the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) went out and recited ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, then went back in. So some of us said to others: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I will recite to you a third of the Qur'an.'" Then the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) came out and said: "I said I would recite to you a third of the Qur'an. Indeed, it is equal to a third of the Qur'an."

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, and others narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By He in whose hand is my soul, it is indeed equal to a third of the Qur'an," meaning ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, and others narrated from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his companions: "Can any of you not manage to recite a third of the Qur'an in a night?" That was hard for them, and they said: "Which of us can do that?" He said: "Allah, the One, the Eternal Refuge, is a third of the Qur'an."

Muslim and others narrated a similar report from the hadith of Abu al-Darda'.

A similar report has been narrated with a sahih chain from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, and the hadith of Umm Kulthum bint Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt. Something similar has been narrated from others with chains, some of which are hasan and some da'if. Even if nothing about the virtue of this surah had been reported except the hadith of Aishah in al-Bukhari, Muslim and others, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) sent a man in a military expedition, and he used to recite to his companions in their prayer and would end with ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾. When they returned, they mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Ask him why he does that.' They asked him, and he said: 'Because it is the attribute of the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it.' He said: 'Tell him that Allah the Exalted loves him.'" This is the wording of al-Bukhari in *Kitab al-Tawhid*.

Al-Bukhari also narrated in *Kitab al-Salah* from the hadith of Anas, who said: "A man from the Ansar led them in prayer at the Mosque of Quba'. Whenever he began a surah which he recited to them in the prayer, he would open with ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ until he finished it, then he would recite another surah with it. He did this in every rak'ah. His companions spoke to him and said: 'You open with this surah, then you do not consider it sufficient until you recite another with it. Either recite it or leave it and recite another.' He said: 'I will not leave it. If you wish that I lead you in this manner, I will do so; and if you dislike it, I will leave you.' They regarded him as one of their best, and they disliked that anyone other than him should lead them. When the Prophet (ﷺ) came to them, they informed him of the matter. He said: 'O so-and-so, what prevents you from doing what your companions command you, and what made you persist in this surah in every rak'ah?' He said: 'I love it.' He said: 'Your love for it has admitted you to Paradise.'" This wording has been narrated through other routes outside al-Bukhari with the same meaning.

**In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate**

His words: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾. The pronoun (huwa, "He") may refer to what is understood from the context, because of what we have already mentioned about the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul, the circumstances in which a verse was revealed), namely that the polytheists said: "O Muhammad, trace for us the lineage of your Lord." In that case, huwa is the subject (mubtada'), "Allah" is a second subject, "One" (ahad) is the predicate of the second subject, and the whole clause is the predicate of the first subject.

It is also possible that "Allah" is an apposition (badal) to huwa, and the predicate is "One."

It is also possible that "Allah" is the first predicate and "One" the second predicate.

It is also possible that "One" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is One."

It is also possible that huwa is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), because it is a place of glorification, and the clause after it explains it and is a predicate concerning it. The first view is the more preferred.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Huwa is a metonymy for the mention of Allah, and the meaning is: if you ask for an explanation of ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, it is said..." The hamzah in ahad (aḥad) is a replacement for a waw, and its original form is wahid (wāḥid, "one").

Abu al-Baqa' said: "The hamzah of ahad is original in itself, not transposed (maqlubah)." He mentioned that ahad conveys universality (al-'umum), unlike wahid.

Among the things that show the difference between them is what al-Azhari said: that no one other than Allah the Exalted is described as ahadiyyah (absolute oneness), and one does not say "a man (rajul) ahad" or "a dirham ahad," as one says "a man wahid" or "a dirham wahid."

It was said that wahid enters into ahad, but ahad does not enter into wahid. Therefore, when you say "no one wahid can withstand him," it is permissible to say "but two can withstand him," unlike your saying "no one ahad can withstand him."

Tha'lab distinguished between wahid and ahad by saying that wahid enters into the counting of numbers, while ahad does not enter into it.

Abu Hayyan refuted him by saying that one says "ahad wa 'ishrun" (eleven) and the like, so the number has entered it. "And this, as you see, is..." Among those who held the view of transposition (qalb) was al-Khalil.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ with the affirmation of qul (Say).

(p. 1668) Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy read "Allah, the One" without qul.

Al-A'mash read "Say: He is Allah, the Wahid (the One)."

The majority read ahad with tanwin (nunation, the "-un" ending), which is the original form.

Zayd ibn Ali, Aban ibn Uthman, Ibn Abi Ishaq, al-Hasan, Abu al-Simmak, and Abu Amr in one narration from him read it with the tanwin dropped, for lightness (li al-khiffah), as in the words of the poet:

*'Amru alladhi hashama al-thariyda li-qawmihi / wa-rijalu Makkata musnitūna ʿijāfu*

("'Amr, who crumbled the bread for his people, while the men of Mecca are famine-stricken and lean.")

It was said that the omission of tanwin is because it meets the definite article (al-), so the omission is to avoid the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). This is answered by saying that avoiding the meeting of two unvocalized letters has already occurred with the tanwin, by vocalizing the first of them with a kasrah.

﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge (al-Samad)﴾. The noble Name is the subject (mubtada'), and al-Samad is its predicate. Al-Samad is the one to whom one turns (yusmad) in needs, that is, who is sought because He is able to fulfil them. It is thus a form (fa'al) in the meaning of a passive participle (maf'ul), like al-qabd meaning al-maqbud (the grasped), because He is the one to whom one turns, that is, the one who is sought. Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-Samad is the lord (sayyid) to whom lordship has ended, so there is no lord above him."

The poet said:

*Ala bakkara al-na'iyu bi-khayri Bani Asad / bi-ʿAmri ibn Mas'udin wa-bi-l-sayyidi al-samad*

("Has not the messenger of death (al-na'i) hastened at dawn with the news of the best of the Banu Asad, ʿAmr ibn Mas'ud, and of the lord, al-Samad?")

It was said that the meaning of al-Samad is the one who lasts, remains, who has always existed and never ceases.

It was said that the meaning of al-Samad is what is mentioned after it, that He is the One who neither begets nor is born.

It was said that He is the one who is free of need of anyone, while everyone is in need of Him.

It was said that He is the one who is the aim in desires and the one sought for help in calamities. These two sayings return to the meaning of the first saying.

It was said that He is the one who does what He wills and judges what He intends.

It was said that He is the Perfect, who has no defect.

Al-Hasan, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid, Abdullah ibn Buraydah, Ata', Ata'iyyah al-Awfi, and al-Suddi said: al-Samad is the solid (al-musmat), which has no hollow within it. From this is the poet's saying:

*Shihabun harubun la tazalu jiyaduhu / 'awabisa ya'lukna al-shakima al-musammada*

("A meteor (shihab), fierce, whose steeds never cease, grim, chewing the bit that is solid and hardened.")

This is not incompatible with the first opinion, since it is possible that this is the original meaning of al-Samad, and then it was used for the lord (sayyid) to whom one turns in one's needs. For this reason the lexicographers and the majority of the exegetes (ahl al-tafsir) agreed upon the first opinion. From it is the saying of the poet:

"I struck him with a sword, then I said to him: Take it, O Ḥudhayf, for you are the sayyid al-ṣamad."

And al-Zibriqan ibn Badr said:

"Travel together at midnight and press on, and there is no hostage except a sayyid ṣamad."

The repetition of the noble name serves to indicate that whoever does not possess this attribute is far removed from deserving divinity (al-ulūhiyyah). The conjunction is omitted from this sentence because it is like the conclusion (natījah) of the first sentence. It was said that al-Samad is an attribute of the noble name and the predicate (khabar) is what follows it, but the first is preferable, because the context requires that each sentence be independent.

﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾, that is, no offspring issues from Him, and He does not issue from anything, because nothing is of His kind, and because it is impossible to attribute non-existence to Him, whether before or after.

Qatadah said: The polytheist Arabs said, "The angels are the daughters of God," the Jews said, "ʿUzayr is the son of God," and the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of God." So God refuted them and said: ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾. Al-Razi said: The mention of the negation of offspring was placed first, although offspring is normally placed first for emphasis, because of what the disbelievers were saying: the polytheists said that the angels are God's daughters, the Jews said that ʿUzayr is God's son, and the Christians said that the Messiah is God's son, while no one claimed that He has a parent. For this reason He began with the more important matter, saying ﴿He begets not﴾, then He pointed to the proof, saying ﴿nor is He begotten﴾, as if it were said: the proof that offspring is impossible is our agreement that He was never the offspring of anything else. God, glory be to Him, expressed it with something that indicates the negation of His being one who begets or is begotten in the past, and did not mention what indicates the negation of that in the future, because it came as an answer to their saying "God has begotten," as God related of them in His saying: ﴿Surely they say, out of their own lying, "God has begotten"﴾ [al-Saffat: 151–152]. Since the purpose of this verse is to refute their saying, and they only said that with a wording that indicates negation regarding the past, the verse came to repel this saying of theirs.

﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾. This sentence confirms the content of what precedes it, because when He, glory be to Him, is characterized by the attributes mentioned earlier, He is characterized by the fact that no one is equal to Him, none resembles Him, and none shares with Him in anything. The subject of "kāna" (was) is placed last for the sake of the rhyming endings (fawāṣil). The phrase "lahu" (for Him) is related to "kufuwan" (comparable), and it is placed before it for emphasis, because the intended meaning is the negation of equality from His essence.

It was said that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial (ḥāl), but the first is preferable.

Al-Mubarrad refuted Sibawayh with this verse, because Sibawayh said that when the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) precedes, it is the predicate, while here it was not made the predicate despite being placed first. Al-Mubarrad's refutation was answered in two ways. The first: Sibawayh did not make this an absolute rule, but permitted it. The second: we do not accept that the adverbial phrase here is not a predicate; rather it may be a predicate, and "kufuwan" is accusative as a circumstantial. It is reported in al-Kashshaf from Sibawayh that the eloquent Arabic usage is to place after the adverbial phrase that is a non-fixed complement (laghw ghayr mustaqirr), and this report only transmitted the beginning of Sibawayh's statement and did not look to its end, for he said at the end of his statement: "Placing first, placing last, treating as a complement, and treating as fixed are good, common Arabic." End of quote.

The majority read "kufuwan" with a damma on the kaf and the fa and easing of the hamza. Al-A'raj, Sibawayh, and Nafi' in one narration from him read it with the fa sukūn, and this was reported from Hamzah, with the hamza changed to a waw both in pause and in continuation. Nafi' in another narration read "kifa'" with a kasra on the kaf and a fatha on the fa without elongation, and Sulayman ibn ʿAli ibn ʿAbdullah ibn al-ʿAbbas read it likewise with elongation. And he recited the verse of al-Nabighah:

"Do not hurl me with a pillar for which there is no kifa'."

In the language of the Arabs, the kufu' is the equal; one says "this is your kufu'," i.e., your equal, and the noun is kafa'ah with a fatha.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Mahamili in his Amali, al-Tabarani, and Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah reported from Buraydah, "I do not know it except as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report," he said: al-Samad is the one who has no hollow (jawf). This marfu' attribution is not authentic.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Mas'ud, he said: al-Samad is the one who has no hollow, and in another wording: He has no entrails.

Ibn Abi ʿAsim, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported from Ibn ʿAbbas the like of this.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him, he said: al-Samad is the one who does not eat, and it is al-mussamat (the solid, having no hollow). And he said: Have you not heard the mourning woman saying:

"The announcer has come early with the best of Banu Asad, with ʿAmr ibn Masʿud and with the sayyid al-samad."

He used to not eat during fighting. It has also been reported from him that it is the one to whom one turns in needs, and that he recited the verse and argued with it for this meaning. This meaning is more apparent in praise and more fitting for nobility, and his description as one who does not eat during fighting has little meaning.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat reported through the chain of ʿAli ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: al-Samad is the sayyid who has perfected his lordship, the noble who has perfected his nobility, the great who has perfected his greatness, the forbearing who has perfected his forbearance, the self-sufficient (ghani) who has perfected his self-sufficiency, the almighty (jabbar) who has perfected his might, the knowing who has perfected his knowledge, the wise who has perfected his wisdom; He is the one who has perfected all kinds of nobility and lordship, and He is God, glory be to Him. This is an attribute that befits none but Him; there is no equal to Him, and there is nothing like Him.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi reported from Ibn Mas'ud, he said: al-Samad is the sayyid whose lordship has reached its end, so there is nothing more lordly than Him.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh in al-ʿAzamah reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: al-Samad is the one to whom things turn when distress or calamity befalls them.

Ibn Jarir reported through several routes from him, regarding His saying ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾, he said: He has no equal and no likeness.
